title: Taking an Uber, Part 5: The Long Ride Home
culturalNote: The last ride with Kamau — and by now you can banter like a local. Kenyan conversation is seasoned with methali (proverbs) and idioms. "Haraka haraka haina baraka" (hurry hurry has no blessing) when someone's rushing; "Kawia ufike" (delay, but arrive) when you're late; "Umeniwacha kwa mataa" (you left me at the traffic lights) when someone stood you up. Using one at the right moment earns instant respect — and a laugh.
startingPoint: Friday night, 10 p.m. You're heading home from a party in Westlands. Kamau picks you up — late, again.

turns.speaker: Mteja
turns.swahili: Kamau! Umeniwacha kwa mataa! Nimekuwa nikikungoja kwa dakika arobaini!
turns.english: Kamau! You left me hanging! I've been waiting for you for forty minutes!

words.gloss: "You left me hanging!" — lit. "you left me at the traffic lights": when someone doesn't show up or leaves you stranded.
by / with / at / for / to (very flexible — see explainer)
minute — n/n noun (same word for one & many)
40 (n/n form — used for counting, money, things)

turns.speaker: Dereva
turns.swahili: Pole sana, boss! Foleni ya Westlands ni mbaya. Lakini, kawia ufike, sivyo?
turns.english: So sorry, boss! The Westlands jam is terrible. But better late than never, right?

words.gloss: boss — friendly, informal way to address a man (driver, guard, waiter) — m/wa noun (people & animals)
"Better late than never" — lit. "delay, but arrive". A proverb.

turns.speaker: Mteja
turns.swahili: Haha! Sawa, kawia ufike. Lakini sasa usiendeshe kwa kasi — haraka haraka haina baraka.
turns.english: Haha! Fine, better late than never. But now don't drive fast — hurry hurry has no blessing.

words.gloss: "Better late than never" — lit. "delay, but arrive". A proverb.
now — also a greeting: "Sasa?" = "What's up now?"
"Don't drive" — u- (subject: you) + si- (not) + -endeshe (drive, subjunctive -e). From kuendesha. Extension: causative (-isha/-esha/-za: "make / cause").
"Hurry hurry has no blessing" — rushing brings mistakes.

turns.speaker: Dereva
turns.swahili: Wee! Kumbe sasa unaongea kama Mkenya halisi! Umenivunja mbavu!
turns.english: Whoa! Oh, so now you talk like a real Kenyan! You've cracked me up!

words.gloss: now — also a greeting: "Sasa?" = "What's up now?"
"You are talking" — u- (subject: you) + na- (present) + -ongea (talk). From kuongea.

"you've cracked me up" — lit. "you've broken my ribs"

turns.speaker: Mteja
turns.swahili: Unatia chumvi! Bado ninajifunza. Lakini mambo ni mengi, muda ni mchache.
turns.english: You're exaggerating! I'm still learning. But so much to do, so little time.

words.gloss: "I am learning" — ni- (subject: I) + na- (present) + -jifunza (learn). From kujifunza. Colloquially often shortened: ni-na- → na-.
things / matters / issues — plural of jambo. "Mambo?" = "What's up?" (lit. "matters?")
"many / a lot" — ji/ma agreement (mambo mengi, magari mengi)

words.gloss: truth — Kenyans give it n/n agreement
"How was it?" — i- (subject: it (n/n)) + li- (past) + -wa (be) + -je (how?). From kuwa.

turns.speaker: Mteja
turns.swahili: Ilikuwa poa, lakini saa nne wakati ulitupa kisogo — kila mtu alikuwa amechoka.
turns.english: It was cool, but at ten time was up — everyone was tired.

words.gloss: "It was" — i- (subject: it (n/n)) + li- (past) + -wa (be). From kuwa.
cool / fine — from kupoa, "to cool down"
"time was up" — lit. "time turned the back of its head (on us)"
"He/she was" — a- (subject: he/she) + li- (past) + -wa (be). From kuwa.
"He/she is tired" — a- (subject: he/she) + me- (perfect (done / now-state)) + -choka (get tired). From kuchoka.

turns.speaker: Dereva
turns.swahili: Haha! Na wiki ijayo, unaenda Mombasa? Ningekuwa najua mapema, ningekupeleka mimi!
turns.english: Haha! And next week, are you going to Mombasa? If I'd known earlier, I would have driven you myself!

words.gloss: "You are going" — u- (subject: you) + na- (present) + -enda (go). From kuenda.
"If I had known" — Kenyan colloquial conditional
"I would take you (somewhere)" — ni- (subject: I) + nge- ("would") + ku- (object: you) + -peleka (take (somewhere)). From kupeleka.

turns.speaker: Mteja
turns.swahili: Ni safari ndefu! Lakini polepole ndio mwendo. Nikikuhitaji, nitakupigia.
turns.english: It's a long trip! But slow and steady is the way. If I need you, I'll call you.

words.gloss: journey / trip — n/n noun (same word for one & many)
"tall / long" — n/n agreement (things; Kenyans use it for most non-people nouns).
"Slow and steady is the way" — lit. "slowly is the (right) pace"
"If/when I need you" — ni- (subject: I) + ki- (if / when · or "-ing" after kuwa) + ku- (object: you) + -hitaji (need). From kuhitaji. After a past kuwa (nilikuwa …) the -ki- form means "…-ing".
"I will call you" — ni- (subject: I) + ta- (future) + ku- (object: you) + -pigia (call). From kupigia. Extension: prepositional (-ia/-ea: "for / to / at").
